hero.subtitle: The original specification for email delivery that established how messages traverse the Internet, still in use (updated) over 40 years later.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) defines the mechanism for transmitting email messages between mail servers. It operates on a store-and-forward model where messages are relayed between Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs).

Jon Postel authored this RFC along with many other foundational Internet standards. SMTP remains one of the oldest protocols still in active daily use, handling billions of emails per day.

sections.title: SMTP Commands
sections.content:
SMTP uses a simple text-based command-response protocol over TCP port 25.

HELOIdentify the sending host
MAIL FROMSpecify the envelope sender
RCPT TOSpecify an envelope recipient
DATABegin the message body
QUITClose the connection
RSETReset the session state
NOOPNo operation (keep-alive)
VRFYVerify a mailbox exists

sections.title: Reply Codes
sections.content:
SMTP reply codes are three-digit numbers where the first digit indicates the class of response:

2xxPositive completion (e.g., 250 OK)
3xxPositive intermediate (e.g., 354 Start mail input)
4xxTransient negative (e.g., 451 Local error)
5xxPermanent negative (e.g., 550 Mailbox unavailable)

sections.title: Legacy and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 821 was updated by RFC 2821 and then RFC 5321, adding extensions like EHLO, STARTTLS, authentication, and internationalized email. The core store-and-forward model remains unchanged.

ESMTP
Extended SMTP (RFC 5321) adds capabilities negotiation via EHLO
STARTTLS
Opportunistic encryption for SMTP connections
SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Authentication mechanisms to prevent email spoofing

references.text: Postel, J., "Simple Mail Transfer Protocol", RFC 821, August 1982.
Klensin, J., "Simple Mail Transfer Protocol", RFC 5321, October 2008.
